# Background and dataset

## Column {width=45%}

::: {.card}
### Project overview

This dashboard presents a computational musicological analysis of my own top songs from **2018 to 2025**, using a merged corpus based on my yearly **“Your Top Songs”** playlists. It asks which musical features remain stable across my listening history, which change over time, and whether these changes suggest gradual shifts in taste or more substantial stylistic reorientation.

The project is guided by three research questions:

1. What are the most common musical features across my top songs?  
2. How do these features evolve over time in my listening habits?  
3. Did my tastes change over the years, and if so, how?  

The merged corpus is used for broad comparisons across years, while the yearly **#1 songs** serve as the main close-reading examples in the more detailed pitch, timbre, harmonic, and temporal analyses. Together, these different levels of analysis make it possible to compare overall listening patterns with close musical detail.
:::

::: {.card}
### Main findings

Across **2018–2025**, my listening history appears **more stable than volatile**. The strongest continuities emerge in **metre, tempo, danceability, and broad feature space**, while the clearest variation appears in **valence, timbre, and local temporal articulation**. Overall, the analyses suggest that changes in taste were mostly **gradual rather than abrupt**, with a few standout tracks acting as exceptions rather than evidence of a complete stylistic break.
:::

::: {.card}
### Representative tracks

The playlist below contains the **#1 song from each year**, which serve as the main close-reading examples throughout the dashboard. These tracks help connect the visual analyses to concrete listening examples, while the full merged corpus remains the basis for broader year-by-year comparison. The playlist is ordered from the year 2025 to 2018.

## Column {width=55%}

::: {.card}
### Corpus overview

Before turning to individual feature domains, this corpus overview shows the overall balance of the dataset and highlights the broad listening patterns that already appear at the track level.

![](Images/Page 1/corpus_overview_page1.png){width=100%}

The corpus is fairly evenly distributed across the years **2018–2025**, which makes year-by-year comparisons more reliable, even if some years may still differ slightly in representativeness. At the broadest level, the feature trends suggest both continuity and change in my listening habits. **Danceability** remains consistently high across the whole period, and **energy** also stays relatively high, which suggests that rhythmically engaging and intense tracks are a stable part of my taste. By contrast, **acousticness** rises over time, especially in the later years, which may indicate a gradual shift toward more acoustic or less densely produced music. **Valence** fluctuates more than the other features, suggesting that the affective tone of my favorite songs changes more from year to year than the basic rhythmic or energetic profile of the music.
:::

# Track-level features {orientation="rows"}

## Row {height=20%}

::: {.card}
### Track-level features

This section examines whether the broad **track-level properties** of my top songs remain consistent across years or reveal gradual changes in taste. Taken together, the boxplots and scatterplots suggest that my listening history is **more stable than volatile**: tempo, energy, and danceability remain concentrated in a similar range across years, while **valence varies more clearly**, indicating that mood shifted more than rhythmic drive or overall intensity.

At the summary level, the boxplots show how yearly distributions and medians change over time. The scatterplots add a second perspective by showing how songs are distributed within a broader feature space. Read together, these figures help distinguish between **stable preferences**, **gradual shifts in emphasis**, and yearly **#1 songs** that may stand out from the wider pattern of listening.
:::

## Row {height=80%}

### Column {width=50%}

::: {.card}
### Tempo and valence across years

![](Images/All top songs/Week 11/tempo_by_year.png){width=100%}

![](Images/All top songs/Week 7/valence_by_year.png){width=100%}

These plots show that my listening habits were **more stable in tempo than in valence**. The yearly tempo boxplots overlap strongly, and the medians remain concentrated in a similar moderate-to-fast range, which suggests continuity in the basic pacing or pulse of the songs I preferred. Valence, by contrast, varies more from year to year: the boxes shift more noticeably, and the yearly **#1 songs** move more clearly between higher- and lower-valence positions. This suggests that the emotional colouring of my favourite tracks changed more than their rhythmic framework.

This difference becomes more meaningful when read alongside the scatterplots on the right. The boxplots show in summary form what the feature clouds later confirm visually: **tempo stays comparatively anchored**, while affective character is more flexible. A careful interpretation is still necessary, since tempo and valence are only track-level summaries and do not capture all aspects of rhythm or expression. Even so, the overall pattern suggests that my taste remained tied to a fairly consistent rhythmic zone, while leaving more room for variation in mood or affective tone.
:::

### Column {width=50%}

::: {.card}
### Energy, danceability, and overall feature space

![](Images/All top songs/Week 7/danceability_energy_by_year.png){width=100%}

![](Images/All top songs/Week 7/audio_feature_overview_by_year.png){width=100%}

These figures place my top songs in a broader **track-level feature space** and reinforce the same story from a different angle. Across most years, the songs cluster in a similar region marked by **moderate-to-high energy and danceability**, while **valence is more dispersed**. This suggests that one stable component of my taste is a recurring preference for songs with rhythmic drive, momentum, and accessibility, even when their emotional tone differs. The strong overlap between yearly clouds indicates that changes in taste were mostly **gradual rather than abrupt**.

Compared with the boxplots on the left, these scatterplots make visible not only yearly change but also the **shape and spread** of my listening profile. They show that stability is not just a matter of similar medians: my songs repeatedly occupy a similar feature region across years. At the same time, the yearly **#1 songs** sometimes fall away from the centre of each cloud, which means that standout favourites were not always fully representative of my broader listening in that year. Taken together, the boxplots and scatterplots suggest that my taste changed less through wholesale shifts in rhythmic or energetic profile and more through **shifts in emphasis within a stable feature space**, especially in the affective dimension represented here by valence.
:::


# Chroma features [pitch] {orientation="rows"}

## Row {height=22%}

::: {.card}
### Chroma features [pitch]

This section examines what **chroma-based features** reveal about my listening history: whether my favourite songs return to similar tonal centres, whether pitch-class activity is organized in similar ways across years, and whether these harmonic tendencies remain stable or change over time.

At the corpus level, the analysis asks whether certain tonal centres recur across the years. At the track level, it compares three yearly **#1 songs** with different global keys — *New Light* (2019), *Dolla Dolla Bill* (2021), and *Ojitos Lindos* (2022) — in order to test whether differently keyed songs still share broader harmonic tendencies, tonal stability, or structural reuse. Taken together, the heatmap, chromagrams, self-similarity matrices, and keygrams show that my listening history is shaped not only by recurring tonal centres, but also by different degrees of harmonic concentration, repetition, and local key stability.
:::

## Row {height=78%}

### Column {width=40%}

::: {.card}
### Pitch overview across the corpus

![](Images/All top songs/Week 8/key by year with n1.png){width=100%}

This heatmap suggests that my listening history contains **recurring tonal centres** rather than a completely different key profile every year. **C#** appears especially prominent across several years, while other years are distributed more evenly across neighbouring keys, which points to continuity with variation rather than one fixed harmonic preference. The yearly **#1 songs** often fall outside the most common key of the year, showing that standout favourites were not always tonally typical of my broader listening.

This figure is most useful as a **corpus-level tonal summary**. It shows that some pitch centres recur across the listening history, but it cannot show local modulation, mode, or how pitch material is distributed inside a song. That is why the three yearly favourites below are used as close-reading cases.
:::

### Column {width=60%}

::: {.panel-tabset .card}

## Chromagrams

**2019 (#1: *New Light*)**  
![](Images/All top songs/Week 8/New light.png){width=100%}

**2021 (#1: *Dolla Dolla Bill*)**  
![](Images/All top songs/Week 8/Dolla Dolla Bill.png){width=100%}

**2022 (#1: *Ojitos Lindos*)**  
![](Images/All top songs/Week 8/Ojitos lindos.png){width=100%}

These chromagrams show how **pitch-class activity unfolds over time inside individual songs** rather than summarizing each track with one global key label. The rows represent the twelve pitch classes, and brighter horizontal bands indicate stronger activity. The main thing to notice is whether pitch energy is spread across many rows or concentrated in a smaller set.

*New Light* shows the broadest and most fluid pitch-class field: activity is distributed across several rows, especially around **A, G, E, D, and C**, which suggests a more open harmonic organization. *Dolla Dolla Bill* is more tightly concentrated, especially around **B, E, G, F#, and D**, giving it a narrower and more repetitive tonal space. *Ojitos Lindos* shows the strongest pitch focus, with repeated emphasis around **C#, F#, Ab, Eb, and Bb**, which creates the clearest sense of a stable harmonic centre and aligns most closely with its global key estimate in the yearly heatmap.

Taken together, these chromagrams suggest that continuity in my listening history is not only about returning to similar key labels, but also about different degrees of **harmonic concentration and stability**. Some favourite songs organize pitch energy broadly, while others return more insistently to a limited pitch-class field.

## Pitch self-similarity

**2019 (#1: *New Light*)**  
![](Images/All top songs/Week 8/2019_New_Light_pitch_self_similarity.png){width=100%}

**2021 (#1: *Dolla Dolla Bill*)**  
![](Images/All top songs/Week 8/2021_Dolla_Dolla_Bill_pitch_self_similarity.png){width=100%}

**2022 (#1: *Ojitos Lindos*)**  
![](Images/All top songs/Week 8/2022_Ojitos_Lindos_pitch_self_similarity.png){width=100%}

These pitch self-similarity matrices show how **harmonic material is reused over time**. The most important places to look are the **off-diagonal paths and blocks**: clearer returns suggest repeated pitch material, while larger darker regions suggest more internally homogeneous passages.

Among the three examples, *Dolla Dolla Bill* shows the clearest repeated sectional structure. *New Light* looks more diffuse, with weaker and less sharply segmented repetition, which gives the form a more continuous character. *Ojitos Lindos* falls between these two cases: it shows noticeable returns, but they are less rigidly patterned than in *Dolla Dolla Bill*. This suggests that my favourite songs differ not only in tonal centre, but also in how clearly and regularly harmonic material is repeated across sections.

## Local key analysis

**2019 (#1: *New Light*)**  
![](Images/All top songs/Week 10/New_Light_keygram.png){width=100%}

**2021 (#1: *Dolla Dolla Bill*)**  
![](Images/All top songs/Week 10/Dolla_Dolla_Bill_keygram.png){width=100%}

**2022 (#1: *Ojitos Lindos*)**

These keygrams show **which local keys become more plausible over time** rather than reducing a whole song to one global label. The main thing to notice is whether brightness stays concentrated around one narrow region or moves across a broader field of related keys.

In *New Light*, the brighter activity is spread across a wider set of related keys, especially around **G major, E minor, C major, and D major**. *Dolla Dolla Bill* is more concentrated around **B major / G# minor**, with nearby emphasis in **E major** and **C# minor**. *Ojitos Lindos* repeatedly gravitates toward **Eb major / C minor**, with nearby emphasis in **Ab major** and **Bb minor**. Taken together, these figures suggest that my listening history is shaped not only by recurring tonal centres, but also by different degrees of **tonal stability** inside songs.
:::






# Loudness and timbre {orientation="rows"}

## Row {height=22%}

::: {.card}
### Loudness and timbre

This section examines two related but distinct dimensions of my listening history: **overall loudness** and **timbral organization**. At the corpus level, the loudness plot asks whether my preferred songs became louder, softer, or more variable across years. At the track level, MFCC heatmaps and timbre self-similarity matrices show how sonic colour is distributed within selected songs and how consistently that colour is repeated across sections.

Taken together, these analyses suggest that my listening history is relatively **stable in overall loudness**, but more varied in **timbral texture and timbral form**. In other words, the general intensity profile of my favourite songs remains fairly consistent across years, while the way songs shape and repeat their sonic colour differs more clearly from track to track.
:::

## Row {height=78%}

### Column {width=35%}

::: {.card}
### Loudness in the corpus

![](Images/All top songs/Week 9/loudness_by_year.png){width=100%}

This plot suggests that the loudness of my preferred songs was **mostly stable over time**, since the yearly medians remain in a fairly narrow range and the distributions overlap strongly from 2018 to 2024. That means there is little evidence of a steady shift toward either consistently louder or consistently softer listening across most of the dataset. The most noticeable differences instead appear in the **spread of the yearly distributions** and in the position of the **#1 songs**.

In most years, the favourite track sits close to the centre of that year’s loudness range, which suggests that the standout song was usually loudness-typical of my broader listening. **2025** is the clearest exception: its #1 song sits well below the yearly core, and the year also contains more very quiet outliers. This points less to a complete change in taste than to a slightly wider openness to softer tracks in recent years.

At the same time, loudness should not be equated with musical intensity more broadly. A track can have a moderate average loudness and still feel powerful because of its arrangement, density, or the way energy is distributed across sections. For that reason, this graph is most useful for showing that my listening habits stayed anchored in a fairly consistent loudness profile, while becoming somewhat more flexible at the quieter end.
:::

### Column {width=65%}

::: {.panel-tabset .card}

## Cepstrograms

**2020 (#1: *Blinding Lights*)**  
![](Images/All top songs/Week 9/2020_Blinding_Lights_timbre.png){width=100%}

**2021 (#1: *Dolla Dolla Bill*)**  
![](Images/All top songs/Week 9/2021_Dolla_Dolla_Bill_timbre.png){width=100%}

**2025 (#1: *NUEVAYoL*)**  
![](Images/All top songs/Week 9/2025_NUEVAYoL_timbre.png){width=100%}

These MFCC heatmaps compare the **timbral profiles** of three yearly favourites by showing how cepstral coefficients change over time. The lower-order coefficients near the bottom are especially important because they summarize the broader shape of the spectral envelope, while higher coefficients capture finer detail. The main thing to notice is whether the lower rows look **smooth, striped, or strongly contrastive** over time.

*Blinding Lights* looks the most even and smoothed, with relatively persistent horizontal bands and fewer abrupt timbral disruptions. *Dolla Dolla Bill* shows stronger local fluctuation, especially in the lower coefficients, with more visible striping and clearer sectional contrast. *NUEVAYoL* appears more restrained for much of the track, but with a more noticeable timbral shift in the later middle section, where the lower coefficients darken and the spectral envelope seems to change more clearly.

Read together, these plots suggest different ways of organizing timbre: **stable and polished** in *Blinding Lights*, **more contrastive and segmented** in *Dolla Dolla Bill*, and **more muted with a clearer internal shift** in *NUEVAYoL*. Compared with the loudness graph, the MFCCs also show that **average loudness and timbral organization are related but not identical**. A quieter track can still have a clearly differentiated timbral design, and a louder track can sound controlled rather than simply dense. This suggests that my listening history was fairly stable in general intensity, but more varied in how sonic colour was shaped over time.

## Timbre self-similarity

**2020 (#1: *Blinding Lights*)**  
![](Images/All top songs/Week 9/2020_Blinding_Lights_timbre_self_similarity.png){width=100%}

**2021 (#1: *Dolla Dolla Bill*)**  
![](Images/All top songs/Week 9/2021_Dolla_Dolla_Bill_timbre_self_similarity.png){width=100%}

**2025 (#1: *NUEVAYoL*)**  
![](Images/All top songs/Week 9/2025_NUEVAYoL_timbre_self_similarity.png){width=100%}

These timbre self-similarity matrices show how each song **reuses its sonic texture over time**. The most important patterns are the off-diagonal blocks and stripes: when these recur clearly, they suggest repeated timbral sections or returns of similar instrumentation and spectral colour.

*Blinding Lights* shows the most regular and grid-like pattern, which suggests a highly controlled and repetitive timbral design. *Dolla Dolla Bill* is also strongly repetitive, but with sharper internal contrasts between sections. *NUEVAYoL* looks less rigidly patterned, with repeated timbral relations that are weaker and more uneven, especially around the later middle of the track. This suggests a structure that is still organized, but less tightly looped than the other two examples.

Compared with the MFCC heatmaps and the loudness plot, these matrices reinforce the same broader conclusion: **loudness and timbral form are connected but distinct**. *Blinding Lights* combines relatively high loudness with strong timbral repetition, while *Dolla Dolla Bill* remains strongly sectioned even without being the loudest of the three. *NUEVAYoL*, which was also the quietest outlier in the loudness analysis, shows a less repetitive and more flexible timbral structure. Taken together, these three examples suggest that my favourites differ not only in how loud they are, but also in how consistently they repeat their sonic colour over time. Across the page as a whole, the strongest conclusion is that **loudness is relatively stable across the corpus, while timbral organization varies more across selected tracks**.
:::



# Temporal features [duration] {orientation="rows"}

## Row {height=22%}

::: {.card}
### Temporal features [duration]

This section examines whether my listening history changed in its **temporal organization**: not only in broad track-level properties such as **metre** and **duration**, but also in the finer internal pacing of songs. At the corpus level, the analysis asks whether my favourite tracks shifted toward different time signatures or song lengths across years. At the track level, novelty curves and tempograms show how strongly songs differ in **local rhythmic change, sectional pacing, and pulse organization**.

Taken together, these analyses suggest that my listening history was **highly stable in metre**, somewhat more flexible in **duration**, and most variable in the **internal organization of pulse and change over time**. In other words, the broad temporal framework of my favourites remained quite consistent, while the way songs articulated movement and contrast within that framework differed more clearly from track to track.
:::

## Row {height=78%}

### Column {width=40%}

::: {.card}
### Corpus-level temporal structure

![](Images/All top songs/Week 11/time_signature_by_year.png){width=100%}

![](Images/All top songs/Week 11/duration_by_year.png){width=100%}

These temporal-feature plots suggest that my listening history was **highly stable in metre** but somewhat more flexible in **song length**. The time-signature chart is dominated almost entirely by **4/4** in every year, and all yearly **#1 songs** also fall into that metre. This means there is little evidence that my taste changed through shifts in basic pulse organization: even when other musical features varied, my favourites remained rooted in the standard quadruple metre that characterizes much popular music.

Track duration shows slightly more variation. Most yearly distributions stay centred around the familiar **3–4 minute** range, which suggests another broad continuity in my listening habits, but some later years include more long-duration outliers. The yearly **#1 songs** usually sit near the middle of their distributions, although **2021** is relatively short, **2022** somewhat longer, and **2025** falls below the centre of a year that otherwise contains several extended tracks. Overall, these graphs suggest that my temporal preferences were **more stable in metre than in length**: the pulse framework stayed consistent, while the amount of time a song occupied became a little more flexible.

This corpus-level stability is important because it sets up the more detailed analyses on the right. If the broad metric frame remains mostly unchanged, then differences in temporal taste are more likely to appear in **how songs distribute change and pulse internally** than in whether they use unusual metres or radically different durations.
:::

### Column {width=60%}

::: {.panel-tabset .card}

## Novelty

**2021 (#1: *Dolla Dolla Bill*)**  
![](Images/All top songs/Week 11/2021_Dolla_Dolla_Bill_novelty.png){width=100%}

**2022 (#1: *Ojitos Lindos*)**  
![](Images/All top songs/Week 11/2022_Ojitos_Lindos_novelty.png){width=100%}

**2025 (#1: *NUEVAYoL*)**  
![](Images/All top songs/Week 11/2025_NUEVAYoL_novelty.png){width=100%}

These novelty curves add a finer-grained temporal view to the earlier time-signature and duration plots. A novelty function highlights moments of local change, so the main thing to look for is **where peaks occur, how tall they are, and whether they are evenly spread or clustered**.

In *Dolla Dolla Bill*, the first half of the excerpt is relatively quiet, but after roughly **14 seconds** the curve becomes much denser and more jagged, with many high peaks. That suggests a passage with more frequent onsets or sharper local changes. *Ojitos Lindos* looks more even and restrained: the peaks are generally lower, more dispersed, and less dramatically clustered, which suggests a smoother local rhythmic flow. *NUEVAYoL* is the most contrastive of the three, because it stays fairly low for most of the excerpt and then produces a strong burst of large peaks in the final third, especially after about **23–24 seconds**.

These three excerpts therefore do not mainly differ in metre, but in how **change and accent density** are distributed over time. This refines the corpus-level result: the dominance of **4/4** suggests continuity in basic pulse organization, but the different peak patterns show that my favourites vary more in how strongly they articulate internal change within that shared framework. *Ojitos Lindos* suggests a steadier and less abrupt temporal profile, while *Dolla Dolla Bill* and especially *NUEVAYoL* create stronger local contrast through clustered bursts of novelty.

## Tempograms

**2021 (#1: *Dolla Dolla Bill*)**  
![](Images/All top songs/Week 11/2021_Dolla_Dolla_Bill_act_tempogram.png){width=100%}

**2022 (#1: *Ojitos Lindos*)**  
![](Images/All top songs/Week 11/2022_Ojitos_Lindos_act_tempogram.png){width=100%}

**2025 (#1: *NUEVAYoL*)**  
![](Images/All top songs/Week 11/2025_NUEVAYoL_act_tempogram.png){width=100%}

These **ACT tempograms** refine the temporal analysis further by showing how strongly different **local pulse rates** are supported over time. The important thing to notice is whether the brighter horizontal bands stay relatively stable or become redistributed across the track. Because pulse is hierarchical, these bands should not be read as one exact “true tempo” only; related pulse levels can appear together.

In *Dolla Dolla Bill*, the most visible bands stay relatively stable across the full track, especially around a slower pulse region near **55 BPM** and its related higher levels, which suggests a fairly consistent periodic framework even when the novelty curve becomes much denser after about **14 seconds**. *Ojitos Lindos* looks more segmented: the stronger tempo bands appear in clearer blocks, with repeated local emphasis around the same pulse region but more obvious sectional interruptions. *NUEVAYoL* shows the greatest late change: the tempogram becomes more active and redistributed in the later portion of the song, which matches the novelty curve’s strong burst of peaks after roughly **23–24 seconds**.

Read together with the novelty curves and the corpus-level plots, the tempograms suggest that these tracks do not mainly differ in **basic metre**, but in **how steadily or flexibly they sustain local pulse energy over time**. In that sense, *Dolla Dolla Bill* combines a stable pulse framework with more abrupt local change, *Ojitos Lindos* combines stable metre with smoother and more sectionally patterned pulse organization, and *NUEVAYoL* keeps the same broad temporal framework but introduces much stronger late contrast in both novelty and tempo-related energy. Across the page as a whole, the strongest conclusion is that my temporal taste was **stable at the level of metre**, somewhat flexible in **length**, and most variable in the **internal organization of pulse and change over time**.
:::

# Clustering {orientation="rows"}

## Row {height=20%}

::: {.card}
### Clustering

This section examines whether my top songs form **meaningful groups** when they are compared across multiple track-level features at once. Rather than focusing on one variable at a time, clustering asks whether the full corpus breaks into distinct listening phases or whether songs from different years still return to overlapping feature families.

Taken together, the dendrogram and clustered heatmap suggest that my listening history is **more continuous than sharply segmented**. Songs from different years often cluster together, which implies that my taste kept returning to similar combinations of musical features over time. At the same time, the clustering also leaves room for a smaller number of outliers or unusual songs, showing that continuity in taste coexists with some distinct exceptions.
:::

![](Images/All top songs/Week 12/week12_dendrogram_coloured_song_names.png){width=100%}

This dendrogram suggests that my top songs form **overlapping groups rather than sharply separated yearly phases**. Songs from different years are mixed throughout the tree, and many tracks from early and later years cluster together at relatively low heights. This means that my listening history is more **continuous than abrupt** in the feature space used here: even when individual yearly favourites differ, the broader set of songs keeps returning to similar combinations of musical properties.

Some songs join very early, which suggests especially close similarity, while a few tracks connect to the rest only at higher levels, meaning they are more distinctive within the corpus. :::

This clustered heatmap displays the **top 10 songs from each year (2018–2025)** and groups them according to similarity across multiple **track-level features**. Each row is a song and each column is one feature: acousticness, instrumentalness, tempo, duration, valence, danceability, speechiness, liveness, energy, and loudness. The colours show whether a song is above or below the overall average for each feature, with brighter cells indicating relatively higher values and darker cells indicating relatively lower values. The dendrogram on the side groups songs with similar feature profiles, so neighbouring rows are alike across the **full combination of features**, not just in one column. Songs from different years appear throughout the same clusters, which suggests that my listening history repeatedly returns to similar feature combinations rather than splitting into sharply distinct phases. A good example is the top part of the heatmap, where *NUEVAYoL* and *The Lamp Is Low* cluster together because they are relatively **quiet, low-energy, and more instrumental/acoustic** than much of the rest of the corpus. This matters for the portfolio as a whole because it reinforces the earlier track-level findings: my listening history seems to be built around a few recurring musical profiles, with some more distinctive songs sitting further away from my usual centre. Together, the dendrogram and heatmap suggest that clustering supports a story of **stable preference families with some exceptional deviations**, rather than sharply separated eras of taste.
:::

# Contribution

::: {.card}
### What this analysis shows

Taken together, the analyses suggest that my listening history is shaped more by **continuity with variation** than by abrupt stylistic breaks. At the broadest level, my top songs repeatedly return to a similar track-level feature space marked by relatively stable **tempo, danceability, energy, and metre**. The clustering analyses reinforce this pattern: songs from different years often group together rather than forming sharply separated yearly phases, which suggests that my taste remained anchored in a limited number of recurring musical profiles. In that sense, the strongest answer to the first research question is that my favourite songs are not randomly distributed across the corpus, but consistently return to a recognisable set of rhythmic, energetic, and tonal tendencies.

At the same time, the project also shows that this stability was **not complete**. The clearest variation appears in features related to **valence, timbre, local temporal articulation, and tonal organization within songs**. The close readings of the yearly **#1 songs** show this especially clearly. The pitch analyses suggest that some tonal centres recur across years, but also that these standout tracks differ in how tightly pitch material is concentrated, how strongly harmonic material is repeated, and how stable local key regions remain over time. The loudness and timbre analyses suggest that overall intensity stayed fairly consistent, while sonic colour and timbral repetition varied more clearly across selected yearly favourites. The temporal analyses lead to a similar conclusion: metre remained highly stable, but the **#1 songs** differed more in sectional pacing, novelty, and pulse organization. Together, these results suggest that changes in taste were less about replacing one musical world with another and more about **rebalancing existing preferences** — especially in mood, texture, tonal focus, and internal rhythmic shape.

The overall contribution of this portfolio is therefore twofold. First, it shows how computational musicology can describe a **personal listening history** in a way that is more precise than anecdotal self-description alone. Second, it demonstrates the value of combining **corpus-level summaries** with **close readings of the yearly #1 songs**: the larger corpus reveals broad continuity, while the detailed pitch, timbre, and temporal analyses show where meaningful differences emerge within that stable frame. This kind of approach could be useful for people interested in computational musicology, personal listening-history research, or reflective analyses of how musical taste develops over time. At the same time, the conclusions should remain cautious: all of these findings depend on the available corpus, the selected features, and the fact that track-level descriptors simplify musical experience. Even so, the main result is clear: my music taste did change across the years, but mostly through **gradual shifts in emphasis within a stable preference structure**, rather than through complete stylistic transformation.
